papers.title: A validation approach for RNA structures based on deep-learning 3D-structure predictions
papers.abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of life depends on accurate macromolecular structures. RNA, in particular, poses a particular challenge for structural biology due to its inherent flexibility and dynamic nature. The challenging nature of structure determination experiments and their interpretation have led to the development of validation approaches to prevent or fix errors in solved structures. Existing methods for RNA structure validation can, as with proteins, be broadly split into two types. Map-based validation tools seek to detect discrepancies between the experimental data and the determined structure. They are excellent for fixing all types of errors, but only when high-resolution experimental data are available.Model-only validation methods, which usually focus on molecular geometry, are excellent for fixing short-length-scale issues even when experimental resolution is low. Conkit-validate is a mapless method for protein validation, which is not based on chemical plausibility, but rather on the similarity between experimental models and structure predictions for the same protein. By comparing contact patterns, this tool leverages evolutionary covariance information, learned by state-of-the-art structural prediction models, into a mapless validation method capable of detecting sequence assignment issues, with notable success in detecting register errors. Here, we extend the conkit-validate method to work on RNA.The results show performance similar to that previously achieved for proteins. %We also show how this new method can detect errors missed by map-based approaches when the experimental data is of low resolution. In a scan of the PDB, its detection rate does not depend on the local resolution of the density, so it remains applicable where map-based approaches are not, and case studies show it can identify register errors where the density alone cannot decide between models.Together, this highlights the complementary value of a contact-prediction based validation approach using information orthogonal to map- and geometry-based approaches to ensure the quality of deposited RNA structures against varying criteria.The performance of the method can be expected to track ongoing improvements in RNA structure prediction methods.

papers.title: irAEGIS: Pathway-guided interpretable prediction of immune-related adverse events
papers.abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are major complications of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy and remain difficult to predict prior to treatment initiation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides a unique opportunity to characterize immune states associated with future irAE development. However, translating single-cell measurements into accurate and biologically interpretable patient-level risk predictions remains challenging. Existing approaches typically aggregate cellular profiles into patient-level summaries, thereby obscuring cell type specific signals, or rely on complex deep-learning architectures that offer limited insight into the biological pathways and mechanisms underlying their predictions. Here, we present irAEGIS, a pathway-guided interpretable model for predicting irAE risk from pre-treatment scRNA-seq data. irAEGIS incorporates prior biological knowledge through gene set constrained representation learning, aggregates pathway activities within individual cell types, and integrates cell type specific risk signals through a hierarchical prediction framework. This design enables predictions to be decomposed into contributions from individual cell types, pathways, and genes, providing interpretable explanations across multiple biological resolutions. Across simulated datasets and independent pre-treatment ICI cohorts, irAEGIS consistently outperformed seven existing methods. Beyond predictive performance, irAEGIS identified biologically coherent immune programs associated with irAE risk. In non-small cell lung cancer, irAEGIS highlighted neutrophil-associated inflammatory pathways linked to future irAE development, whereas in melanoma, it identified apoptotic and immune activation pathways in CD8+ NKT-like cells associated with severe irAEs. These findings were independently supported by pathway enrichment, cell-cell communication, and trajectory analyses. Together, irAEGIS provides a biologically informed and interpretable model for linking single-cell immune states to patient outcomes, enabling both accurate risk prediction and mechanistic insight into immune-related adverse events. More broadly, irAEGIS establishes a general strategy for interpretable phenotype prediction and biological discovery from single-cell transcriptomic data.

papers.title: Aging reshapes cardiac extravascular leukocyte transcription through bidirectional remodeling during LPS-induced endotoxemia
papers.abstract: Sepsis disproportionately affects older adults and is frequently complicated by cardiac dysfunction. However, how aging alters the transcriptional responses of cardiac extravascular immune cells during systemic inflammation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated aging-dependent transcriptional remodeling of cardiac immune cells using an LPS-induced endotoxemia model in young and aged C57BL/6 mice. Mice received intraperitoneal LPS (5 mg/kg body weight) or vehicle, and cardiac extravascular leukocytes were isolated from ex vivo retrogradely perfused hearts 24 h later for single-cell RNA sequencing. Aging was associated with bidirectional transcriptional remodeling, characterized by both up- and downregulation of gene programs, particularly in cardiac macrophages, monocyte-like macrophages, T cells, and B cells following LPS challenge. A shared feature across these four cell populations was reduced representation of mitochondrial-associated transcriptional programs, indicating aging-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial biology across cardiac myeloid and lymphoid lineages during systemic inflammation. In parallel, cell type-specific transcriptional remodeling revealed distinct functional-associated responses. Macrophages and monocyte-like macrophages exhibited increased tissue-remodeling and repair-associated transcriptional programs. Both T and B cells showed reduced metabolic programs but increased actin cytoskeleton organization. T cells additionally exhibited reduced cytotoxicity-associated and enhanced Th17-associated transcriptional programs, whereas B cells showed reduced antigen-processing and presentation programs. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested aging-associated differences in immune cell interactions following LPS challenge and potential features of cardiac inflammaging at baseline. Together, these findings demonstrate that aging bidirectionally reshapes the cardiac immune response to systemic inflammation, characterized by shared remodeling of mitochondrial-associated programs and cell type-specific changes in inflammatory, metabolic, cytoskeletal, and effector-associated programs. These aging-dependent transcriptional changes occurred in the context of the greater severity of illness observed in aged mice following LPS-induced endotoxemia.

papers.title: Continuous Topological Accessibility (RFA) as a 3D-Aware GRN Filter: Anticorrelation with eQTL and No Prediction of ΔRNA
papers.abstract: We formalize Relative Forest Accessibility (RFA), a topological accessibility index computed as the solution of (I - {gamma}P )x = v0, where P is a Markov transition matrix built from Hi-C contacts and v0 is a vector of TF peaks (or ATAC peaks). RFA yields a continuous accessibility profile across all genomic bins. We test RFA on three targets. First, on promoter TF counts (GM12878 chr1, 10 kb, 811 genes), RFA loses to 1D distance (AUC 0.836 vs 0.976); this is an artifact because the target and the 1D distance look at the same window. Second, on eQTL (GTEx v10 LCL, chr1+17+19, 10 kb, 1625 genes), RFA anticorrelates with eQTL: {rho}(RFA, - log10 pmin) = -0.09, AUC(RFA) = 0.386 (below chance), AUC(-RFA) = 0.614. High RFA corresponds to fewer eQTL, and dose-response analysis confirms that AUC(RFA) decreases with eQTL strength (mean trend -0.056, 19/20 TFs). A distance-preserving shuffle of the Hi-C matrix reproduces this anticorrelation ({triangleup}AUC vs real: [-0.074, +0.076] across 5 TFs, all CIs include 0), whereas a degree-preserving rewiring destroys it ({triangleup}AUC [isin] [-0.261, -0.003], CIs exclude 0 for 5/5 TFs); the anticorrelation therefore reflects distance-decay of Hi-C contacts (local 3D accessibility), not higher-order topology. The anticorrelation replicates on chr17 ({triangleup}{rho} = -0.13 for rewired, 0/5 for shuffled) and on chr19 with an inverted control pattern, consistent with local within-diagonal heterogeneity as the carrier on short gene-dense chromosomes. Third, on {triangleup}RNA (MCF10A vs MCF7, 40 kb, ATAC peaks), RFA does not predict {triangleup}RNA ({rho} = +0.005, permutation p = 0.87, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.040, +0.053], n = 1730); the CI includes zero and does not exclude the practical boundary |{rho}| = 0.05. Within-line sanity checks are also null. We conclude that RFA anticorrelates with eQTL via local distance-decay and does not predict {triangleup}RNA. The anticorrelation is carried by distance-decay, not by loops or TADs, and may reflect expression buffering: genes with strong eQTL are less dependent on local 3D accessibility. RFA is not a universal predictor but a filter with an inverted sign on eQTL and no signal on {triangleup}RNA.

papers.title: Res ipSAE adhuc loquuntur: What the directionality of predicted aligned error in cofolding models can tell us about scoring diverse molecular complexes
papers.abstract: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) and Boltz-2 estimate confidence in predicted biomolecular complexes using the interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) score, which is derived from probability distributions of predicted aligned errors (PAEs) between molecular tokens. These errors are directional: the predicted position of tokens in one molecule is evaluated relative to coordinate frames defined by tokens in another. The PAE matrix is therefore asymmetric, but AF3 reports the maximum of the two directional pairwise ipTM scores, whereas Boltz-2 reports them separately. In both programs, the TM-score scaling parameter, d0, depends on molecular system size rather than solely on the component being scored. In protein-protein complexes, including disordered regions and domains unrelated to the interface can further lower ipTM. I previously introduced the interaction predicted score from aligned errors (ipSAE) to address these limitations for protein-protein complexes. Here, I extend ipSAE to interactions involving proteins, nucleic acids, small-molecule ligands, and atomic ions. The framework makes three explicit choices for each molecular pair: which component supplies the alignment frames, which tokens are scored, and how d0 is defined. For different molecular types, I propose aligning on the more complex molecule and scoring the simpler one. For protein-ligand complexes, this entails aligning on protein residues, scoring all ligand heavy atoms without a PAE cutoff, and using a fixed d0 of 2 [A]. In benchmarks of 102 protein-ligand complexes predicted by AF3 and Boltz-2, this ipSAE formulation yields a substantially wider range of confidence scores than native ipTM. On a held-out set of 82 complexes, ipSAE thresholds of 0.5 for AF3 and 0.8 for Boltz-2 classified ligand placements with balanced accuracies of 0.938 and 0.862, respectively, using a ligand RMSD threshold of 5 [A]. Protein-DNA benchmarks support the same directional scoring scheme, while smaller protein-RNA benchmarks provide a preliminary assessment. These results establish a framework for interpreting predicted structural confidence across different classes of biomolecular interactions and suggest that directional scoring may also be useful for computationally designed protein binders. The new freely available ipSAE code is available from: https://github.com/DunbrackLab/IPSAE2.

papers.title: FoXSight: Facilitating Computational Hit Identification in Crystallographic Fragment Screening Experiments
papers.abstract: X-ray crystallographic fragment screening reveals how small molecules bind to proteins, providing important starting points for drug design. Identifying these weak binding events remains difficult when electron density signals are noisy, partially occupied or obscured by solvent, and campaigns may comprise thousands of datasets. Here, we present FoXSight, a computational method for hit identification in crystallographic compound screening. FoXSight applies Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) filtering to multi-reference subtraction maps to detect recurring, target-specific density features associated with bound ligands. Its output maps remain visually interpretable and support subsequent ligand modeling. We evaluated FoXSight on in-house and public datasets spanning seven protein targets, comparing its maps with PanDDA where suitable comparison data were available. FoXSight was successfully used as the primary hit identification tool in a challenging crystallographic fragment screening campaign for human Cathepsin L, where the output of established methods was impractical to inspect systematically.

papers.title: FedEpitope: Parameter-Efficient Federated Protein Language Models for Linear B-Cell Epitope Prediction
papers.abstract: Linear B-cell epitopes are antigenic regions recognised by antibodies that play crucial roles in vaccine development, antibody production, and other therapeutic applications.Their prediction can support peptide-based vaccine candidate screening and diagnostic assay development, but the experimental data required for model development may be distributed across institutions that cannot freely pool their records. We present FedEpitope, a federated framework that adapts the ESM-2 protein language model for peptide-level linear B-cell epitope prediction using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), keeping client-partitioned data local and restricting the communicated trainable model state to approximately 1.11 MB. Simulated benchmarks of FedAvg and FedProx algorithms, evaluated using homology-aware data splits of five biologically heterogeneous, organism-partitioned clients, achieve promising global test performance without centralising training data, with FedAvg outperforming all single-client models in mean AP, F1, and MCC. Additional experiments characterise post-federation personalisation, record-level differential privacy, sensitivity to controlled client heterogeneity, LoRA rank, and generalisation to the independent BCPreds and NetBCE benchmarks, demonstrating the feasibility of parameter-efficient federated protein language model adaptation for data-localised B-cell epitope prediction and the associated trade-offs among predictive performance, personalisation, privacy, communication efficiency, and distribution shift.

papers.title: PHATE-Derived Ancestry Coordinates Capture Continuous Population Structure in Human Genomic Data
papers.abstract: Population genetic data are increasingly visualized using low-dimensional embeddings as ancestry coordinates, yet how these methods represent population structure can depend strongly on sampling and construction choices. Principal component analysis (PCA), when visualized using only leading components, can obscure fine-scale structure, while nonlinear neighbor-based methods such as uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) often fragment geographic and admixture gradients into discrete clusters. Here, we introduce a framework for constructing ancestry coordinates using potential of heat-diffusion for affinity-based trajectory embedding (PHATE), a diffusion-based method that preserves relationships across scales. Across synthetic benchmarks and large genomic datasets, we show that appropriate scale tuning and population balancing allow PHATE to recover geographic organization and admixture gradients. We show that incorrectly tuned neighborhood scale and population imbalance can distort the resulting representations of population structure. These results therefore provide a methodological framework and practical guidance for constructing ancestry visualizations that better reflect continuous human genetic diversity.

papers.title: When perfect is a warning: explanations expose shortcuts that accuracy hides in cancer gene-expression classifiers
papers.abstract: When the classes in a training set come from different data sources, a classifier can score near-perfectly while learning where a sample came from. We show this for cancer classifiers trained on tumours from The Cancer Genome Atlas and normal tissue from the Genotype Tissue Expression project. Six model families, including a tabular foundation model, reached an area under the curve of 1.000 yet called 80 to 97% of tumour adjacent normal tissue cancer, and 100% in an independent cohort; a few matched normal samples per tissue removed most of this shortcut. Near-perfect accuracy could not tell a shortcut from an honestly easy task, flagging 87 to 92% of models trained on such tasks. We introduce a label free score, computed from model explanations, that uses the fact that a source difference looks the same in every tissue whereas cancer changes do not. It raised no false alarms, ranked models by their real reliance on the source, transferred to unseen model types and data, and failed where its theory predicts.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Dual-Target Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery Under Strict Homology Constraints
papers.abstract: The worldwide escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe challenge to modern public health, necessitating novel classes of therapeutic agents. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent highly promising alternatives to small-molecule antibiotics due to their co-evolutionary resilience and rapid membrane disruption dynamics. However, translating computational AMP leads into clinical drug candidates remains bottlenecked by off-target cytotoxicity, predominantly hemolytic activity against mammalian erythrocytes. Although pretrained foundational protein language models (PLMs) have rapidly advanced molecular property prediction, current architectures frequently isolate antibacterial potency and cytotoxicity into disconnected single-task pipelines or succumb to catastrophic performance drops under strict homology-controlled evaluations. Recently, the Quantitative Mapping of Antimicrobial Peptides (QMAP) benchmark proposed that frozen PLM embeddings show weak linearly accessible features for hemolytic activity (HC50) resulting in poor rank correlation ({rho} < 0.25) on out-of-distribution sequence splits. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end multi-task parameter-efficient transfer learning framework designed to simultaneously optimize antibacterial potency and minimize mammalian cytotoxicity without sequence leakage. Built upon ESM-2 (150M), our architecture incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into self-attention projections, fine-tuning approx 0.70% of model weights. To restore gradient interference originating from disparate membrane lysis mechanisms, we implement an adaptive multi-task loss guided by Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. Evaluated across predefined QMAP benchmark splits enforcing a 60% maximal sequence identity threshold, our joint architecture remarkably outperforms conventional linear probes, tree-based regressors, and frozen foundational models. The framework achieves an E. coli potency rank correlation of {rho} = 0.6132 (r = 0.6816) and successfully elevates hemolytic toxicity correlation to {rho} = 0.5374 (r = 0.5541). To establish real world utility, we deploy the optimized joint network to screen a curated in silico library of 749 de-novo designed peptides, successfully isolating selective cationic-amphipathic candidates possessing Therapeutic Indices (TI = HC50/MIC) up to 144.03 while effectively deprioritizing broadly lytic motifs (TI < 2.0). These findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient adaptation unlocks fine-grained bioactive structural semantics in foundational PLMs, providing an accurate, scalable framework for therapeutic peptide engineering.

papers.title: A compact motif vocabulary is differentially interpreted across human cell types
papers.abstract: How a common genome generates diverse human cell types may depend less on distinct cis-regulatory vocabularies than on context-dependent use of a shared one. We have developed CNN-CR, an interpretable neural network that learns regulatory motifs while predicting gene expression across 116 human biosamples. Promoter regulation proves highly compressible: dozens of recurrent motif families retain most of the predictive information of much larger cell-type-specific vocabularies and generalize to cellular contexts excluded from their discovery. These motifs are conserved at their binding sites and enriched at fine-mapped regulatory variants. Cellular context acts at two levels: chromatin state gates which motif instances are available for regulatory use, whereas reader identity determines how accessible motifs are interpreted. ChIP-seq data reveal frequent shifts in reader occupancy across cell types, and genome-scale perturbations support corresponding context-dependent reader functions. Thus, regulatory diversity can emerge through differential access to and interpretation of a compact shared DNA vocabulary.

papers.title: NEPTUNE: a neuronal cell death pathway prediction tool used to decipher neurodegeneration using single cell RNA-seq datasets
papers.abstract: In the constantly evolving landscape of cell death mechanisms, much of the literature is dominated by research performed in cancer cells and regenerating cell types. However, neurons differ in that they are non-regenerating and post-mitotic. Therefore, assessing neuronal specific disease biomarkers, including cell death markers, without the bias of non-neuronal or cancerous cells, could provide a more biologically accurate neurodegeneration profile. In this study, we developed the Neuronal cEll death Prediction Tool for Understanding Neurodegenerative Events (NEPTUNE), a user-friendly tool for researchers that bioinformatically identifies neuronal cell death markers from user provided differentially expressed gene lists obtained by single cell RNA sequencing data. We applied NEPTUNE to a publicly available single cell RNA sequencing dataset and analysed the progression of photoreceptor degeneration in the rd1 mouse model of severe retinitis pigmentosa. The analysis interpreted the dataset in a neuronal-specific manner and showed that late-stage photoreceptor death is not purely apoptotic but possibly engages overlapping cell death programmes. From the analysis, the user is provided with publishable graphs and a list of cell death markers with fold change, type of impact, cell death type and a strength score. Overall, our tool provides markers specific to neurodegeneration, allows mapping to known WikiPathways and KEGG pathways, performs GO and KEGG enrichment analysis and plots the data for further analysis, greatly facilitating the study of neuron specific degeneration. The tool can be found at: https://neptune.rgtcarvalholab.com/.

papers.title: Consensus methods for trees of blobs and level-1 phylogenetic networks
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic networks are increasingly used to represent evolutionary histories involving hybridization, introgression, and other reticulate processes that cannot be captured by a single tree. Recent advances have produced numerous methods for inferring networks from genomic data. These methods may produce multiple plausible networks due to optimality ties, bootstrap analyses, Bayesian posterior samples, or differences in tools, datasets, and parameters. While consensus methods are well established for trees and some approaches exist for rooted networks, no consensus framework currently exists for semi-directed (unrooted) networks. We address this gap by introducing a new consensus framework for phylogenetic networks, rooted or semi-directed. We first develop a method for constructing a consensus tree of blobs, taking as input networks of any complexity. Building on this approach, we construct a consensus for level-1 networks (i.e., networks with non-overlapping cycles). This method, called 'L1N consensus', takes a collection of level-1 networks as input and returns a level-1 network. The different components of this consensus network (e.g., blobs, hybrid clades, and edges) have support values that correspond to the frequency of the given component among the input networks. These methods are implemented in PhyloSummaries, building on the foundation of PhyloNetworks. We evaluate the performance of L1N consensus using large-scale simulated data. Our results demonstrate that L1N consensus outperforms existing methods in the rooted setting in terms of informativity and accuracy. Similar results are obtained in the semi-directed setting. Applying L1N consensus to Leopardus and HIV datasets confirms these findings and demonstrates the usefulness of the method.

papers.title: CMVAE: Contrastive Supervision Improves Single-Omic Latent Manifold for Breast Cancer Survival Prognosis
papers.abstract: High-dimensional omics data are vital for fore- casting patient prognosis in oncology. While deep multi-omics learning methods are increasingly popular, they suffer from data missingness and low patient overlap across modalities. Consequently, advancing single-omic representation learning re- mains a critical yet challenging research problem. Standard generative dimensionality reduction methods rely on recon- struction objectives that optimize the global manifold topology; however, overlook downstream clinical outcomes. To address these limitations, we introduce a Contrastive Masked Denois- ing Variational Autoencoder (CMVAE), a self-supervised dual- optimization framework designed to map single-omic information into a clinical outcome-aware latent space. A stochastic feature masking strategy corrupts the input omic profiles, and CMVAE is optimized to simultaneously infer missing molecular data and contrastive alignment of patient survival trajectories. We evaluate CMVAE using leak-proof five-fold stratified cross-validation on the TCGA Breast Invasive Carcinoma (BRCA) cohort. The method outperforms traditional unsupervised methods, achieving an AUROC of 0.7397 {+/-} 0.0239 on patient prognosis. Further analysis demonstrates a highly significant (p < 0.0001) risk stratification among low vs. high risk groups. Beyond comparing within single-omic methods, CMVAE outperforms six state-of- the-art multi-omics survival baselines by a minimum of 3%. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/CMVAE. Note: Accepted at the IEEE BIBM 2026 workshop RLPD-Bio (Representation Learning and Pattern Discovery for Bioinformatics and Biomedicine).

papers.title: Top2All: Benchmarking sparse-to-transcriptome reconstruction from high-expression profiles across sex- and sex-steroid-defined conditions
papers.abstract: Transcriptome-wide profiling at single-cell resolution is limited by sparse detection of gene expression, raising the question of how much transcriptomic information can be recovered from a small set of highly expressed genes. We developed Top2All, a Mouse-Geneformer-based framework for reconstructing transcriptome-wide expression from sample-specific sparse inputs. Using 24 cell-number-normalized RNA-seq profiles of mouse adrenal zona fasciculata cells across eight experimental conditions defined by sex and sex-steroid milieu, we evaluated condition-aware and no-condition models under replicate-wise out-of-fold and leave-one-condition-out validation. Top2All achieved near-unity sample-wise correlation with measured expression, but similarly high correlations were obtained using simple reference profiles, whereas gene-wise evaluation revealed substantially greater differences among methods. Explicit condition information did not consistently improve reconstruction, indicating that sex- and sex-steroid-associated condition information was already strongly encoded in the sparse expression profiles. Nearest-neighbor retrieval provided a stronger baseline than learned reconstruction, and input-depth analysis showed that increasing the number of input genes did not monotonically improve performance. These findings show that a relatively small set of highly expressed genes contains substantial information about transcriptomic state, while accurate reconstruction of gene-specific biological variation remains challenging. Sparse-to-transcriptome models should therefore be evaluated using gene-wise metrics, strong reference baselines, and tests of generalization beyond conditions represented during training.

papers.title: Prefrontal cortex transcriptomes distinguish Alzheimers disease from asymptomatic amyloid pathology, neuropeptide loss, immune-complement activation and glial remodelling
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now defined biologically by cortical amyloid-{beta} (A) and tau (T) pathology, yet the transcriptional programmes that separate symptomatic AD (A+T+) from amyloid-positive, tau-negative pathology ageing (A+T-) and from pathology-free controls (A-T-) remain incompletely resolved in the association cortex. We re-analysed bulk RNA-sequencing data from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) of 15 donors (BioProject PRJNA1017546; 87 sequencing runs aggregated to donor level): Normal (n = 2), pathology ageing (n = 5) and AD (n = 8). Differential expression was tested with DESeq2 (adjusted P 1), and up- and down-regulated gene sets were analysed separately by Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG over-representation. APOE and TREM2 p.Arg47His contrasts were treated as exploratory. AD versus Normal yielded 341 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; 223 up, 118 down) and AD versus pathology ageing yielded 496 (358 up, 138 down), whereas pathology ageing versus Normal yielded only six. Genes reduced in AD were dominated by neuropeptide and hormone signalling (VGF, VIP, CRH, GRP, TAC1, PENK; neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, adjusted P = 8.8 x 10-5; neuropeptide hormone activity, adjusted P = 6.3 x 10-8), most of which also differed from pathology ageing. Genes increased in AD were enriched for interferon-{gamma} response, myeloid activation, adaptive immunity and classical complement (C1QA, C1QB, C1QC). Relative to pathology ageing, AD additionally showed induction of gliogenesis, oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination programmes (gliogenesis, 21 genes, adjusted P = 2.6 x 10-6; SOX10, MYRF) and of the microglial purinergic receptor gene P2RX7 (log2FC = 1.46, adjusted P = 1.5 x 10-5). All six pathology-ageing DEGs, including the myeloid genes VSIG4 and CD163, were also DEGs in AD, and 50 DEGs shared by the two AD contrasts moved in the same direction. Genotype-stratified analyses were underpowered or confounded with diagnosis. In the DLPFC, AD is therefore characterised by a graded loss of neuropeptidergic signalling, myeloid-complement activation that begins at the pathology-ageing stage, and an AD-specific glial/oligodendrocyte response. These signatures nominate candidate biomarkers and mechanisms for early intervention, but the small cohort demands replication in larger, covariate-annotated datasets.

papers.title: GraphExperiment: infrastructure for high-dimensional quantitative data and associated networks in R/Bioconductor
papers.abstract: Networks are widely used to represent relationships among features (e.g. genes, proteins, and microbial taxa) and among observations (e.g. cells, samples, and species) in omics data, as well as their neighborhoods. The Bioconductor ecosystem provides users and developers with modular and interoperable software tools by relying on standard data structures that are reused across packages. However, Bioconductor lacks a standard data structure to store such networks together with the quantitative data from which they are inferred. Here, we present GraphExperiment, an R/Bioconductor package that provides an S4 class extending SingleCellExperiment with containers for feature- level (rowGraphs) and observation-level (colGraphs) networks stored as igraph objects. Networks are kept in sync with assays, row and column metadata, allowing the simultaneous manipulation of quantitative data and graphs. We demonstrate GraphExperiment in seven use cases covering bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell proteomics, microbiome, and comparative genomics data, with networks ranging from gene coexpression and protein co-abundance networks to cell-cell communication and phylogenetic networks. GraphExperiment is available on Bioconductor (https://bioconductor.org/packages/GraphExperiment).

papers.title: Refining RNA-Seq Transcriptome Profiles with Transcript-Specific Minimal-Shared Regions
papers.abstract: Accurate transcript quantification remains a critical challenge in RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) due to ambiguities in read assignment caused by shared regions among transcripts. Beyond shared exons among homologous isoforms, we identified the widespread presence of extensive undefined shared regions-overlapping sequences common to exons or transcripts of heterologous genes-across diverse species, including animals and plants. To overcome this issue, we developed a minimal-sharing strategy that partitions transcripts into unique sets of k-mers and systematically evaluates overlap across all transcripts. By isolating minimal-shared regions specific to each isoform, our approach reduces mapping uncertainty, thereby minimizing false positives and false negatives in transcript detection. Comprehensive evaluations using both in silico simulations and empirical sequencing data demonstrated that our method outperforms traditional probabilistic model-based quantification methods. This strategy improves isoform abundance estimates, enhances gene ontology annotations, and identifies distinct transcript isoforms critical for understanding biological processes, as exemplified in a Huntington's disease mouse model.

papers.title: SENgEAR: an interactive visualization platform for comparative analysis of senescence signatures and cellular communication
papers.abstract: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets provide tremendous potential to identify the cellular states and communication networks associated with senescence. Annotating senescent cells in these datasets is hindered by the lack of universal markers for senescent cells and their context-dependent variability. To overcome this, several groups have developed gene signatures to annotate cells with distinct senotypes. However, comparing these signatures and their biological contexts to determine the specificity of senescence signatures remains complicated by the separate data platforms for signatures and datasets. We present SENgEAR, a no-code web platform for senescent cell annotation, visualization of cell-cell communication networks, and comparison of senescence signatures across studies, tissues, species, and data modalities. SENgEAR provides a unified framework to explore contextual signature specificity, cellular communication pathways, and senotype heterogeneity. We demonstrate the use of SENgEAR for applications spanning aging, fibrosis, and wound healing and its ability to interrelate these states.

papers.title: Peripheral Exercise Transcriptomes Do Not Converge on Glutamatergic or Neuroinflammatory Signatures: A Cross-Platform Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Executive dysfunction following physical overtraining has been linked to glutamatergic dysregulation in the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC), but whether this central mechanism is reflected in peripheral gene expression is unknown. This study tested whether peripheral transcriptomic responses to exercise converge on the glutamatergic or neuroinflammatory pathways implicated in LPFC dysfunction. Three publicly available GEO datasets spanning skeletal muscle, whole blood, and circulating neutrophils were analyzed across four exercise groups using limma, with a discovery threshold of nominal p < 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change above 0.5. Differential expression analysis identified 7,311 unique differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across the four contrasts, but overlap between datasets was limited: 7 genes were shared between skeletal muscle and blood, 38 between skeletal muscle and the GSE43856 contrasts, and 90 between blood and the GSE43856 contrasts, with none significant across all three studies. Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment of the DEG union identified ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis, ribosome biogenesis, protein folding, and T cell activation as the dominant biological processes; no glutamatergic or neuroinflammatory terms reached significance. Cross-tissue concordance between skeletal muscle and blood was absent (r = 0). Effect sizes among the genes driving the top enriched pathways were dominated by ribosomal proteins, heat shock proteins, and translation initiation factors rather than glutamate receptors or transporters. These findings indicate that peripheral transcriptomic responses to exercise are tissue-specific and dominated by proteostasis, translational, and immune programs rather than glutamatergic signaling. Direct assessment of central nervous system tissue or fluid-based glutamatergic biomarkers may be required to link overtraining-induced fatigue to LPFC dysfunction.

papers.title: ToxINsight: An Integrated Web Platform for Sequence, Structure, and Ligand Binding Analysis of Snake Venom Toxins
papers.abstract: Around 5.4 million people worldwide are bitten by snakes each year, with 1.8 to 2.7 million cases of envenomation, of which 81,410 to 137,880 people die from snake envenomation worldwide each year. It is categorized as a high-priority Category A Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) by the World Health Organization (WHO). A molecular level understanding of snake venom toxins and their mechanisms of action is crucial for development of efficient therapeutics tackling snake envenomation. Snake venoms are complex mixtures of bioactive peptides and proteins that have also served as templates for drug discovery. Resources dedicated to snake venom toxins sequence, structure, functions, geographical distributions and molecular-level analysis remain fragmented across general-purpose repositories. Here we present ToxINsight, an integrated, freely accessible database and web-based analysis platform built exclusively for snake venom toxins. ToxINsight curates 2,078 toxin entries spanning 11 medically and scientifically relevant snake toxin families across 237 venomous snake species from five different snake families, and provides 2,540 three-dimensional structures associated with these entries, which are assembled from the RCSB Protein Data Bank , AlphaFold DB and ESMFold-generated 3D models. ToxINsight offers built-in tools alongside toxin records for comparisons and analysis of toxin sequences and structures and their properties for efficient target selection and prioritization. ToxINsight allow the user to select multiple entries and align them, or select a pair of entries to compare structural and physicochemical properties. ToxINsight provides all reported-ligand annotations for each toxin entry, and bulk export of sequence, structure, and metadata for building sequence and/or structure based machine learning models . ToxINsight also offers a visual ATLAS, which provides geographical information about venomous snake families/species for a more focused understanding of snake venom toxins across different geographical landscapes. By combining sequence, structure, ligand and geographical information along with analysis and comparative tools in a single interface, ToxINsight is designed to support and encourage researchers across the world towards the development of efficient targeted therapeutics against snake venom toxins from diverse families. It provides an interface for integrated understanding toxin sequences, structures and physicochemical properties, for providing scaffolds for designing antivenom and for comparative venomics. ToxINsight is freely accessible at https://toxinsight.in/.

papers.title: scRM: A single-cell foundation model trained on scRNA-seq reads
papers.abstract: To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at https://github.com/altos-labs/scRM.

papers.title: A single-cell multimodal foundation model enables cross modality analysis between transcriptome and chromatin
papers.abstract: Most single-cell studies measure either gene expression or chromatin accessibility, and connecting the two usually requires fitting a model to each study. Here we present MUTUAL (MUltiome Transfer in a Unified Aligned Latent space), which keeps the single-cell foundation models scFoundation and EpiAgent frozen, combines their embeddings with linear summaries of each modality and learns a shared RNA--ATAC space from 3.0 million paired cells of 400 public multiome datasets. Applied without refitting to ten datasets not used for training, MUTUAL matched cells' RNA and ATAC profiles more accurately than methods fitted on other donors of the same dataset, annotated ATAC-only cells more accurately and transferred transcription-factor motif activity to RNA-only cells beyond what cell-type assignment provides. In a maturation series of stem-cell-derived islets, motif activity predicted from RNA largely reproduced the measured stage-wise changes when other libraries of the series served as the reference. MUTUAL makes public multiome data directly usable by single-modality studies.

papers.title: A multidimensional benchmark of confounder-aware differential abundance strategies for single- and multi-cohort microbiome studies
papers.abstract: Confounding is a pervasive challenge in microbiome differential abundance analysis (DAA), yet systematic benchmarks of confounder-aware DAA remain lacking. Existing benchmarks have also largely evaluated statistical methods or analytical components in isolation rather than the complete analytical strategies used in practice. We evaluated 71 single-cohort strategies spanning default and extended input configurations using 2,500 real-data-informed simulations, reference-based recovery of established biological signals and resampling-based within-dataset consistency; benchmark-prioritized strategies were further assessed for stability under systematic perturbations. We further evaluated 63 multi-cohort extensions using simulations with cohort heterogeneity and empirical datasets. Covariate adjustment improved false-discovery control at the cost of reduced sensitivity, while performance also depended strongly on the specific combination of preprocessing procedure and statistical model. Different strategies were favored across benchmark dimensions and analytical objectives. ANCOM-BC2_CSS and edgeR_CSS were favored for high-confidence, perturbation-stable inference, whereas ANCOM-BC2_count and ANCOM-BC2_TMM provided more balanced performance. In multi-cohort settings, mega-analysis provided the strongest overall balance when individual-level data were available: ANCOM-BC2_CSS_Mega and edgeR_CSS_Mega showed stronger accuracy performance, whereas ANCOM-BC2_TMM_Mega and ANCOM-BC2_count_Mega showed greater cross-cohort consistency. We implemented these findings in xConDA, an interactive web server linking analytical objectives and study designs to benchmark-prioritized, confounder-adjusted microbiome DAA workflows.

papers.title: Local fractal dimension as an indicator of functional reorganization in molecular interaction networks
papers.abstract: Changes in protein abundance incompletely describe how molecular perturbations reshape cellular organization. Here we introduce DIFFRACT, a framework that integrates quantitative proteomics with protein-protein interaction networks to identify reorganization through changes in local fractal dimension. Molecular associations define effective distances between connected proteins, allowing the geometry of their surrounding network neighborhoods to be compared across conditions. Analyses across four organisms (E. coli, A. thaliana, C. elegans, and H. sapiens) and three interaction resources (STRING, BioGRID, and IntAct) establish heterogeneous local scaling, while controlled perturbations demonstrate sensitivity to regional changes and invariance to uniform distance rescaling. Applied to RAVER1-deficient A549 cells, DIFFRACT identifies components associated with established RNA-regulatory functions and candidate roles in tRNA biology, mitochondrial organization and ciliogenesis. Selected RNA-regulatory and ciliary themes are not significantly enriched by abundance-ranked gene set analysis, supporting complementary information from network geometry. Selected functional annotations also recur in HEK293T cells. Guided by the ciliary predictions, we show that RAVER1 depletion increases the proportion of ciliated A549 cells 2.57-fold and increases cilium length. DIFFRACT thus connects changes in molecular network geometry to experimentally testable biological responses, extending the interpretation of proteomic perturbations beyond differential abundance.

papers.title: Predicted condensation-related signatures localize to two C-terminal regions of the prion protein across cervid PRNP variants associated with chronic wasting disease
papers.abstract: Genetic variation in cervid PRNP influences chronic wasting disease (CWD) susceptibility and progression, but it remains unclear whether disease-associated substitutions produce localized differences in sequence-derived properties relevant to prion protein (PrPC) condensation. We compared a white-tailed deer (WTD) reference sequence with 10 modeled variants on the same mature PrP scaffold (residues 24-233). For each sequence, we calculated intrinsic disorder, FuzDrop per-residue droplet-promoting propensity (pDP) and binding-mode entropy (Sbind), predicted residue-level pKa values, and a discrete-charge summary at pH 7.0. The overall profiles preserve a long N-terminal droplet-promoting region, whereas variant-associated differences are concentrated in selected intervals. In the FuzDrop outputs, residues 126-140 show allele-dependent changes in pDP near the droplet-promoting threshold, and residues 220-230 show variant-specific changes in Sbind, including lower Sbind for S225F/Y and higher Sbind for elk-like Q226E. These differences occur without large changes in overall intrinsic disorder. KaML pKa predictions identify near-neutral titratable sites that provide electrostatic context for these local predictor differences. Independent atomistic simulations of monomeric PrP further detected variant-sensitive backbone behavior and intramolecular contacts involving these intervals. Together, the analysis identifies residues 126-140 and 220-230 as computationally defined candidate intervals that overlap regions implicated independently in prion conversion or CWD fibril structure, motivating direct tests of cervid PrP condensation and maturation.

papers.title: TSNR: Protein-Specific Signals with Broad Molecular Context for Spatial Protein Prediction
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics measures transcriptome-wide gene expression while preserving tissue organization, enabling prediction of spatial protein abundance beyond directly measured antibody panels. Such prediction draws on protein-specific transcript signals at the center spot and broader molecular context from the surrounding tissue. Existing spatial methods increasingly use context, but what molecular information the context should retain and how reliably it transfers across tissue environments remain unclear.We compare predictors that share a protein-specific center representation but differ in contextual molecular scope. Their transferred risk difference admits a value-mismatch characterization: broader context is favored when its target-side value advantage exceeds the corresponding change in source-to-target transfer mismatch. For convex prediction objectives, we further relate mismatch to cross-environment estimating-score variation; squared loss yields an explicit covariance geometry. This analysis motivates broad molecular context together with bounded-score robust regression. We develop Target-Specific Niche Regression (TSNR), which combines a protein-specific center representation, compact broad molecular context, and a protein-specific Huber regressor.On the six-section Spatial-CITE-seq benchmark, TSNR achieves the highest mean macro Spearman correlation among the reproduced methods under matched biological holdout evaluation. Controlled analyses support both broader context and robust regression. Across two independent external cohorts, protein-level broad-context gains are positively rank-correlated with the value-mismatch balance in all 11 held-out biological folds.

papers.title: MaCADEMIA: a software toolbox for single-molecule fluorescence image quantification
papers.abstract: Single-molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM) is a powerful tool in molecular and cellular biology and part of the broad umbrella of super-resolution microscopy. A distinct feature of SMLM, is its capacity for deep quantification, beyond just spatial information, to copy number, stoichiometry, molecular interaction and dynamics in living cells. The hardware required is increasingly straightforward to implement. However, complexity remains in the image analysis where much remains fragmented across specialised software tools. Here, we present MaCADEMIA (Matlab Computational Analysis of Diffusion, Emitter Molecular Intensity and Abundance), a simple yet powerful toolbox of MATLAB functions and associated documentation to enable straightforward extraction of quantitative single-molecule information. MaCADEMIA performs ensemble particle detection achieving localisation accuracies down to 0.5 pixels Root mean squared error (RMSE) across wide signal-to-noise (SNR) ranges on standardised particle tracking benchmarks, consistently matching or exceeding the performance of 14 leading methods. Our integrated workflow enables molecular counting and stoichiometry determination through stepwise photobleaching analysis, mobility measurement via mean squared displacement, colocalisaton analysis and absolute protein copy number quantification using three-dimensional cellular models.

papers.title: SpaceBlocks: an expert-supervised workflow for cohort-level spatial transcriptomics analysis
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has become a central tool in tissue biology, with multiple technologies addressing the issue from a different angle. Each platform imposes its own raw data format conventions, and few workflows address reproducible, scalable, cohort-level analyses while integrating expert-supervised decisions to strengthen computational and biological provenance. In this work, we present SpaceBlocks, a Snakemake workflow for reproducible cohort-level analysis of single-cell resolution-ST data that prioritizes expert supervision over full automation. SpaceBlocks homogenizes heterogeneous platform outputs into a common data format, whose structure is validated to ensure downstream processing. Comprehensive expert supervision is facilitated through per sample quality control and cell type annotation diagnostic visualizations, after which downstream analyses automatically follow. SpaceBlocks also allows the ingestion of technology-agnostic externally formatted data and provides interoperability with existing tools and technologies. We demonstrate the use of SpaceBlocks through the reanalysis of 37 samples from public Visium HD, Xenium 5K and MERSCOPE datasets. SpaceBlocks exhibited processing scalability across the three platforms. This reanalysis identified previously missed cell types in Visium HD and heterogeneous marker gene expression in MERSCOPE, highlighting the need for expert-supervised annotations. Moreover, SpaceBlocks facilitated the identification of differentially expressed genes associated with previously defined multiple sclerosis (MS) spatial domains in MERSCOPE, and transcriptional differences between healthy and malignant colorectal tissues in Visium HD. Together, these findings establish SpaceBlocks as a flexible and reproducible workflow for expert-supervised spatial transcriptomics analysis across technologies and biological cohorts.

papers.title: The Almond Expression Atlas: A comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource for almond gene expression
papers.abstract: Background: Improving crop adaptation and enhancing agronomic and quality traits requires a deeper understanding of gene expression regulation, for which expression atlases are valuable tools. Almond (Prunus dulcis (Mill.) D.A. Webb) is one of the most economically important tree nut crops worldwide. However, an integrated transcriptomic resource for this species is still lacking. Available data remain fragmented across independent studies, limiting their comparability and reuse. Results: Here, we present the first almond gene expression atlas: a comprehensive multi-tissue transcriptomic resource integrating publicly available RNA sequencing data. A total of 142 high-quality untreated and control samples from 17 independent projects were curated through a metadata standardization process and analyzed using a unified bioinformatics pipeline. Standardized expression profiles were generated for 25,225 annotated genes in the Prunus dulcis Texas v2.0 reference genome. The atlas integrates two complementary expression approaches: a median TPM approach capturing quantitative expression levels and a rank-based strategy implemented using the Bgee expression calling method, designed to improve comparability across heterogeneous datasets. This design enables the identification of tissue-specific candidate genes and the exploration of expression patterns across tissues and developmental stages. Its applicability is demonstrated through two use cases, highlighting its ability to identify biologically meaningful gene sets associated with bud dormancy transitions and to prioritize candidate reference genes for RT-qPCR normalization in almond. Conclusions: The Almond Expression Atlas v1.0 is publicly available through FruitDBase (fruitdbase.csic.es), providing an interactive platform for gene expression exploration and visualization. This resource supports functional genomics studies and facilitates candidate gene discovery in almond, while ensuring data traceability and promoting data reusability.
